specStatements.text: Metals react with oxygen to produce metal oxides. The reactions are oxidation reactions because the metals gain oxygen.
Students should be able to explain reduction and oxidation in terms of loss or gain of oxygen.

When metals react with other substances the metal atoms form positive ions. The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions. Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity in a reactivity series. The metals potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron and copper can be put in order of their reactivity from their reactions with water and dilute acids.
The non-metals hydrogen and carbon are often included in the reactivity series.
A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound.
Students should be able to:

recall and describe the reactions, if any, of potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron and copper with water or dilute acids and where appropriate, to place these metals in order of reactivity
explain how the reactivity of metals with water or dilute acids is related to the tendency of the metal to form its positive ion
deduce an order of reactivity of metals based on experimental results.
The reactions of metals with water and acids are limited to room temperature and do not include reactions with steam.
Unreactive metals such as gold are found in the Earth as the metal itself but most metals are found as compounds that require chemical reactions to extract the metal.
Metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by reduction with carbon.
Reduction involves the loss of oxygen.
Knowledge and understanding are limited to the reduction of oxides using carbon.
Knowledge of the details of processes used in the extraction of metals is not required.
Students should be able to:
interpret or evaluate specific metal extraction processes when given appropriate information
identify the substances which are oxidised or reduced in terms of gain or loss of oxygen.
Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons.
write ionic equations for displacement reactions
identify in a given reaction, symbol equation or half equation which species are oxidised and which are reduced.

scopeNotes.statement: The reactions of metals with water and acids are limited to room temperature and do not include reactions with steam.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every reaction with water in this material is a reaction with cold water at room temperature, and every acid reaction uses dilute acid at room temperature. Magnesium is therefore described as reacting only very slowly with cold water, and no item asks for observations, products or equations for any metal with steam. No stem heats a metal in water or supplies steam, and no correction relies on steam chemistry.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge and understanding are limited to the reduction of oxides using carbon.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every extraction item uses a metal oxide heated with carbon. No item asks about electrolysis, about reduction by hydrogen or by a more reactive metal, or about sulfide or carbonate ores. Where a metal above carbon is discussed, students are asked only to conclude that carbon reduction will not work, never to name or describe the alternative method.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of the details of processes used in the extraction of metals is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks for blast furnace zones, temperatures, charge composition, slag formation, plant design or industrial economics. Where a specific process appears it is only as supplied information in the stem, and the question tests the chemical principle drawn from it - the position of the metal relative to carbon, and which substance gains or loses oxygen.

concepts.definition: A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. When a metal reacts with oxygen the metal gains oxygen, so the metal is oxidised.
A reaction in which a substance loses oxygen. When a metal oxide is heated with carbon the oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced.
The compound formed when a metal reacts with oxygen, for example magnesium oxide from magnesium burning in air.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen together: oxygen lost by one substance is gained by another.
A list of metals arranged in order of their reactivity, deduced from their reactions with water and with dilute acids.
The readiness with which a metal atom loses its outer electrons to become a positive ion. The greater this tendency, the more reactive the metal.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound.

concepts.term: Carbon and hydrogen in the series
concepts.definition: The two non-metals often included in the reactivity series as reference points; carbon sits between magnesium and zinc, hydrogen between iron and copper.

concepts.term: Reaction of a metal with water
concepts.definition: A reaction at room temperature giving a metal hydroxide and hydrogen, shown by potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium, and only very slowly by magnesium.

concepts.term: Reaction of a metal with dilute acid
concepts.definition: A reaction giving a salt and hydrogen, shown by magnesium, zinc and iron; copper does not react with dilute acid.
A metal found in the Earth as the element itself rather than as a compound, because it is very unreactive; gold is the standard example.
A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extracting the metal worthwhile.
Heating the oxide of a metal that is less reactive than carbon with carbon, so that the carbon takes the oxygen and the metal is left.
The loss of electrons by a species during a reaction.
The gain of electrons by a species during a reaction.
An equation showing only the species that change in a reaction, with spectator ions left out.
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, for example Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu.
An ion present in the reaction mixture that is unchanged by the reaction and is therefore omitted from the ionic equation.

misconceptions.question: In 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2, what does it mean to say the copper oxide is reduced?
misconceptions.correct: The copper oxide loses its oxygen to the carbon.
misconceptions.misconception: Reduced means there is less of it, so the solid has simply got smaller or lighter.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English 'reduce' means to make smaller, and the solid in the crucible really does lose mass, which seems to confirm the guess.
misconceptions.correction: In chemistry reduction has a fixed meaning: loss of oxygen. The mass falls because oxygen has been removed, but the falling mass is a consequence, not the definition.

misconceptions.question: Copper is heated in air and turns black. Has the copper been oxidised?
misconceptions.correct: Yes - the copper has gained oxygen, so it has been oxidised.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxidation only counts when a substance bursts into flame, and copper does not burn, so nothing was oxidised.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxidation is first met through dramatic burning demonstrations, so students tie the word to visible flames rather than to the gain of oxygen.
misconceptions.correction: Oxidation is defined by the gain of oxygen, however quiet the reaction looks. Copper heated in air gains oxygen to form copper oxide, so it is oxidised.

misconceptions.question: Magnesium burns in air to leave a white powder. What is the white powder?
misconceptions.correct: Magnesium oxide, a new compound of magnesium and oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: It is just magnesium with oxygen mixed into it, so no new substance has been made.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The powder still comes from the same lump of metal, and students who have just studied mixtures reach for the idea that is freshest.
misconceptions.correction: The metal and oxygen are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio and the product has completely different properties. A metal oxide is a compound, not a mixture.

misconceptions.question: Iron gains oxygen when it rusts. Is the iron oxidised or reduced?
misconceptions.correct: The iron is oxidised, because it has gained oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: The iron is reduced, because gaining oxygen is what reduction means.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two labels are learnt as a pair and easily attach to the wrong half; 'reduce' feels like it should describe the change happening to the named substance.
misconceptions.correction: Fix the definitions to the oxygen, not to the substance: gain of oxygen is oxidation, loss of oxygen is reduction. Iron gains oxygen, so iron is oxidised.

misconceptions.question: What happens to a substance that is reduced?
misconceptions.correct: It loses oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: The student equates the '-oxide' in the name with being oxidised: because oxidation means gaining oxygen and the metal oxide is the oxygen-containing compound, they decide iron oxide is the substance that has gained oxygen and so is the one oxidised.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the two terms are opposites but not which way round, and 'reduction' has no obvious link to oxygen in ordinary language.
misconceptions.correction: Reduction is the loss of oxygen; oxidation is the gain of oxygen. In metal extraction the ore is reduced because oxygen is taken away from it.

misconceptions.question: In 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2, is anything oxidised as well as reduced?
misconceptions.correct: Yes - the copper oxide is reduced and the carbon is oxidised in the same reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: A reaction is either an oxidation or a reduction, so only one of the two can be happening.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words are taught in separate lessons and as separate definitions, so students file them as alternatives rather than as two halves of one change.
misconceptions.correction: Oxygen removed from one substance has to go somewhere. Whenever something loses oxygen, something else gains it, so reduction and oxidation occur together.

misconceptions.question: When a metal reacts, what kind of ion does the metal atom form?
misconceptions.correct: A positive ion, formed by losing electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: A negative ion, because the atom takes electrons from the other substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reactions are seen as metals 'attacking' other substances, and taking rather than giving feels like the aggressive option.
misconceptions.correction: Metal atoms have few outer electrons and lose them. Losing negative electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion carries a positive charge.

misconceptions.question: Why is potassium more reactive than magnesium?
misconceptions.correct: Potassium loses its outer electron more readily than magnesium loses its outer electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Potassium must hold on to its electrons more tightly, and that strong grip is what makes it reactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Reactive' is heard as 'strong', and holding on tightly sounds strong, so the reasoning runs the wrong way round.
misconceptions.correction: Reactivity of a metal is its tendency to form positive ions. The more easily a metal gives up its outer electrons, the more reactive it is.

misconceptions.question: Can you predict a metal's reactivity from how dense or how hard it is?
misconceptions.correct: No - reactivity depends on the tendency of the metal to form positive ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Reactivity follows the physical properties: a hard, dense metal is a strong, reactive metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Physical properties are the ones students can see and handle, so they are borrowed to explain a chemical property that has no visible cause.
misconceptions.correction: Sodium is soft and light yet extremely reactive; iron is hard and dense yet far less reactive. Reactivity is about electron loss, not hardness or density.

misconceptions.question: A magnesium atom reacts with dilute acid. What happens to the atom?
misconceptions.correct: It loses two electrons and becomes a magnesium ion.
misconceptions.misconception: It stays as a neutral atom and simply joins on to the other substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture reaction as sticking particles together, so nothing needs to change inside the atom.
misconceptions.correction: When metals react the metal atoms form positive ions. Electrons are transferred away from the metal, so the atom does not survive unchanged.

misconceptions.question: How does a metal atom become positively charged?
misconceptions.correct: By losing negatively charged electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: By gaining protons, since protons are the positive particles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge is correctly linked to protons, and the quickest way to add positive charge seems to be to add protons.
misconceptions.correction: Protons are locked in the nucleus and never move in chemical reactions. Removing electrons leaves the proton count unchanged but the overall charge positive.

misconceptions.question: Zinc is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Which metal ends up as the solid metal?
misconceptions.correct: Copper, because the more reactive zinc displaces it from the solution.
misconceptions.misconception: The student reads the reactivity series backwards, believing the LESS reactive metal displaces the more reactive one from its solution, so they expect copper to push zinc out of a zinc salt solution; and when ranking metals they place the least reactive, calmest metal at the top.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reactivity series is remembered as a list without a direction, so students read it upside down and let the weaker metal do the displacing.
misconceptions.correction: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a compound. Zinc is above copper, so zinc takes its place and copper metal is deposited.

misconceptions.question: Will copper displace magnesium from magnesium sulfate solution?
misconceptions.correct: No - copper is less reactive than magnesium, so no reaction occurs.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes - any metal can displace any other metal from its solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Displacement is remembered as something metals do, without the condition that decides whether it happens at all.
misconceptions.correction: Displacement only happens one way. The metal added must be above the metal in the compound in the reactivity series, otherwise there is no reaction.

misconceptions.question: Calcium loses two electrons and potassium loses one. Which is more reactive?
misconceptions.correct: Potassium is more reactive, even though it loses only one electron.
misconceptions.misconception: Calcium must be more reactive because it loses twice as many electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: More electrons lost looks like more chemistry happening, so quantity is mistaken for ease.
misconceptions.correction: Reactivity depends on how readily electrons are lost, not how many. Potassium's single outer electron is lost far more easily than calcium's two.

misconceptions.question: Does a heavier metal atom mean a more reactive metal?
misconceptions.correct: No - relative atomic mass does not set the order of reactivity.
misconceptions.misconception: Reactivity increases with relative atomic mass, so copper and iron beat sodium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Within a single group reactivity does increase down the group, and students over-extend that pattern across the whole series.
misconceptions.correction: The reactivity series runs potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, copper - light sodium is far above heavy copper.

misconceptions.question: Why are carbon and hydrogen shown in the reactivity series?
misconceptions.correct: They give reference points that metals can be compared against.
misconceptions.misconception: They are shown because they are really metals that behave oddly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everything else in the list is a metal, so students assume membership of the list implies being a metal.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon and hydrogen are non-metals. They are included so that metals can be compared with them, which is what decides how a metal is extracted.

misconceptions.question: Why is carbon placed in the reactivity series?
misconceptions.correct: So that metals can be compared with carbon, which decides if carbon can extract them.
misconceptions.misconception: Because every ore contains carbon, so carbon has to be in the list.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Coke appears in the blast furnace and carbonate ores contain carbon, so carbon seems to be part of the ore itself.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon is placed in the series purely for comparison. Metals below carbon can be reduced by it; metals above it cannot, whatever the ore contains.

misconceptions.question: Can carbon be used to extract every metal from its oxide?
misconceptions.correct: No - only metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted this way.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes - carbon will reduce any metal oxide if it is heated hot enough.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon reduction is the only extraction method studied in detail, so it is taken to be universal.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon can only take oxygen from a metal that holds it less strongly than carbon does. Metals above carbon, such as potassium, need a different method.

misconceptions.question: In 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2, which substance is oxidised?
misconceptions.correct: The carbon, because it gains oxygen to form carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon is the reducing agent, and the student thinks a reducing agent 'gives up' or loses oxygen; knowing that the reducing agent is the substance that is oxidised, they conclude carbon is oxidised because it loses oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon is described as the reducing agent, and the word 'reducing' next to 'carbon' is read as a label for what happens to the carbon.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the definition to the oxygen. Carbon gains oxygen, so carbon is oxidised even though it is the substance that reduces the copper oxide.

misconceptions.question: Why is iron oxide heated with carbon rather than heated on its own?
misconceptions.correct: Because carbon is needed to remove the oxygen from the iron oxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the heat just melts the ore and lets the iron run out of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The furnace is obviously hot and molten metal pours out, so the change looks like melting rather than a chemical reaction.
misconceptions.correction: Iron in an ore is chemically combined with oxygen. Melting cannot separate them; a reduction reaction with carbon is needed to take the oxygen away.

misconceptions.question: Why is gold found in the Earth as the metal itself?
misconceptions.correct: Because gold is so unreactive that it does not readily form compounds.
misconceptions.misconception: Because gold is rare, so there is too little of it to react with anything.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rarity and being found as the metal are two facts learnt about gold together, so one is used to explain the other.
misconceptions.correction: How much of a metal there is has no bearing on whether it reacts. Gold is found native because it is very unreactive, not because it is scarce.

misconceptions.question: Why is gold not found combined as an oxide?
misconceptions.correct: Because gold is too unreactive to combine with oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: Because gold is so dense that it sinks below the ores and stays pure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Panning for gold works by density, so density becomes the explanation for everything about gold.
misconceptions.correction: Density explains how gold is separated from sand, not why it is uncombined. Being unreactive is what keeps gold as the free metal.

misconceptions.question: How did unreactive metals come to be in the Earth as the metal itself?
misconceptions.correct: They were never combined, because they are too unreactive to form compounds.
misconceptions.misconception: They were reduced by carbon underground before anyone dug them up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon reduction is the extraction story students know, so it gets used to explain native metals as well.
misconceptions.correction: Native metals such as gold were never oxidised in the first place. No reduction is needed because no compound formed.

misconceptions.question: Does zinc react with cold water?
misconceptions.correct: No - zinc shows no reaction with water at room temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes - all metals fizz in cold water, some faster than others.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The dramatic demonstrations use potassium, sodium and lithium, and students generalise from the metals they have actually seen react.
misconceptions.correction: Only the metals from magnesium upwards react with cold water, and magnesium only very slowly. Zinc, iron and copper show no reaction with water at room temperature.

misconceptions.question: Copper is used for water pipes. What does this tell you about copper and water?
misconceptions.correct: That copper does not react with water at room temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: That copper must react with water, since it is always in contact with it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Being used with water is read as evidence of a relationship with water, rather than of the absence of one.
misconceptions.correction: Copper is chosen for pipes precisely because it does not react with the water it carries. Contact is not reaction.

misconceptions.question: Iron rusts in damp air. Does iron react with cold water in the laboratory?
misconceptions.correct: No - iron shows no reaction when placed in cold water at room temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes - rusting proves that iron reacts with cold water quite quickly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rusting is the one iron-and-water change students know, and it is assumed to be the same reaction as the ones being compared here.
misconceptions.correction: Rusting needs both water and oxygen and takes days or weeks. In the reactivity test with cold water, iron gives no hydrogen and no reaction.

misconceptions.question: What are the products when magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnesium oxide and hydrogen, because metals form oxides when they react.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Metal oxides dominate the earlier work on oxidation, so the oxide is the product students expect from any metal reaction.
misconceptions.correction: A metal reacting with a dilute acid gives a salt and hydrogen. With hydrochloric acid the salt is the chloride, so magnesium chloride forms.

misconceptions.question: Does magnesium plus dilute hydrochloric acid produce water?
misconceptions.correct: No - the products are magnesium chloride and hydrogen only.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes - acid reactions always give a salt plus water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The neutralisation pattern acid + base -> salt + water is learnt thoroughly and then applied to a metal, which is not a base.
misconceptions.correction: Acid plus metal gives salt plus hydrogen. Only acid with a metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate produces water.

misconceptions.question: Which gas is given off when zinc is added to dilute hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Chlorine, because chlorine is part of hydrochloric acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name of the acid contains 'chloric', so the gas released is assumed to be the chlorine that is named.
misconceptions.correction: The chloride stays behind in the salt, zinc chloride. The gas released is hydrogen, which pops with a lighted splint.

misconceptions.question: Does copper react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
misconceptions.correct: No - copper is below hydrogen, so there is no reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes - every metal fizzes in acid and gives off hydrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Magnesium, zinc and iron all fizz, so the rule 'metal plus acid gives hydrogen' is taken to have no exceptions.
misconceptions.correction: A metal only displaces hydrogen from an acid if it is above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Copper is below hydrogen and does not react.

misconceptions.question: Copper is left in dilute hydrochloric acid. Does the acid turn blue?
misconceptions.correct: No - copper does not react with dilute acid, so the acid stays colourless.
misconceptions.misconception: The acid turns blue because the copper dissolves to give a copper salt.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper compounds met in class are blue, so any container holding copper is expected to turn blue.
misconceptions.correction: A blue solution would need a copper compound to form, and no reaction occurs at all. Copper is below hydrogen and dilute acid leaves it unchanged.

misconceptions.question: Copper in dilute acid shows nothing at all. What does that mean?
misconceptions.correct: There is no reaction between copper and dilute acid.
misconceptions.misconception: There is a reaction, but it is far too slow to see any bubbles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'No reaction' feels like an unsatisfying answer, so students assume something must be happening below the limit of sight.
misconceptions.correction: Copper does not react with dilute acid at all. No reaction is a valid and important experimental result, and it places copper below hydrogen.

misconceptions.question: Two metals are compared. Does the one with more electrons react faster?
misconceptions.correct: No - what matters is how readily the outer electrons are lost.
misconceptions.misconception: The metal whose atoms contain more electrons in total is more reactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reactivity is linked to electrons, so students reach for the electron number they can count from the atomic number.
misconceptions.correction: Only the outer electrons are transferred. Copper atoms have far more electrons than sodium atoms yet copper is much less reactive.

misconceptions.question: A metal shows no bubbles at all in dilute acid. Where does it go in the series?
misconceptions.correct: At the bottom - no reaction means it is the least reactive metal tested.
misconceptions.misconception: At the top, because a metal strong enough to resist the acid must be the most reactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Unreactive' is heard as weak and 'resists attack' is heard as strong, and the two readings pull in opposite directions.
misconceptions.correction: Reactivity is measured by how readily the metal reacts. A metal that does not react at all with dilute acid is the least reactive of the set.

misconceptions.question: A metal gives no reaction with water or with dilute acid. Can it be placed in the series?
misconceptions.correct: Yes - the absence of a reaction places it below the metals that did react.
misconceptions.misconception: No - a metal that does not react gives no information, so it cannot be ranked.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat a negative result as a failed experiment rather than as evidence.
misconceptions.correction: A negative result is evidence. Showing no reaction where others do react places the metal at the bottom of the order.

misconceptions.question: A displaces B, and B displaces C. What can you say about A and C?
misconceptions.correct: A is more reactive than C, so A would displace C as well.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing - A and C were never tested together, so they cannot be compared.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students stick strictly to what was observed and do not see that the two results chain together into one order.
misconceptions.correction: The results give a single order: A above B above C. That order lets you predict the untested pair, and the prediction can then be checked.

misconceptions.question: In terms of electrons, what is oxidation?
misconceptions.correct: Oxidation is the loss of electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxidation is the gain of electrons, since oxidation means gaining something.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oxidation is first learnt as gain of oxygen, so 'gain' becomes attached to the word and is carried over to electrons.
misconceptions.correction: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain - of electrons. A substance that loses electrons is oxidised; one that gains electrons is reduced.

misconceptions.question: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-. What has the zinc lost?
misconceptions.correct: Two electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Two protons, which is why the charge on the ion is 2+.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 2+ charge is correctly linked to positive particles, and protons are the positive particles students name first.
misconceptions.correction: The half equation shows 2e- released, so the zinc has lost two electrons. Proton number never changes in a chemical reaction.

misconceptions.question: In Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, are both species losing electrons?
misconceptions.correct: No - zinc loses electrons and the copper ion gains them.
misconceptions.misconception: Both species lose electrons, because both are changing during the reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electron loss is the half of the definition students recall first, and it gets applied to everything that changes.
misconceptions.correction: Electrons transferred from one species must be gained by another. Oxidation and reduction are two halves of the same electron transfer.

misconceptions.question: In Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, is the copper ion oxidised or reduced?
misconceptions.correct: It is reduced, because it gains two electrons to become copper metal.
misconceptions.misconception: It is oxidised, because it turns into a metal you can see forming.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A visible product looks like the main event, and students label the change they can see as the oxidation.
misconceptions.correction: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu shows electrons being gained, and gain of electrons is reduction. The copper ion is reduced.

misconceptions.question: What should an ionic equation for a displacement reaction show?
misconceptions.correct: Only the species that change - the metal and the metal ion.
misconceptions.misconception: The full formulae of both compounds, including the sulfate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The full symbol equation is written first and the sulfate is copied straight across without asking whether it changed.
misconceptions.correction: Sulfate ions are unchanged spectators, so they are left out. The ionic equation shows only Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu.

misconceptions.question: Is Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg+ + Cu a correct ionic equation?
misconceptions.correct: No - magnesium forms Mg2+, and the charges must balance.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes - it shows magnesium becoming an ion and copper becoming a metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Attention goes to which substances appear rather than to the charges, so an unbalanced charge slips through unnoticed.
misconceptions.correction: Charge must balance across an ionic or half equation. Magnesium loses both outer electrons, so the correct equation is Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu.

misconceptions.question: Is 2Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu a correct ionic equation?
misconceptions.correct: No - putting a 2 in front of Mg unbalances the magnesium atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: A number can be put in front of a formula to make the charges match up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing symbol equations is done by adjusting big numbers, so the same move is tried when the charges do not look right.
misconceptions.correction: Big numbers balance atoms, not charges. Charge is balanced by using the correct ion, Mg2+, so the equation is Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu.

misconceptions.question: The blue colour of copper(II) sulfate solution fades when magnesium is added. Why?
misconceptions.correct: Because copper ions are being removed from the solution as copper metal.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the solution has been watered down or the colour has spread out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fading is associated in everyday life with dilution or with a stain spreading, so a physical explanation is reached for first.
misconceptions.correction: Nothing has been added to dilute the solution. The blue colour fades because the blue copper ions are used up and replaced by colourless magnesium ions.

misconceptions.question: Iron oxide is heated with carbon and iron is obtained. What does that show about iron and carbon?
misconceptions.correct: Iron is less reactive than carbon, so carbon can take the oxygen from it.
misconceptions.misconception: Iron is more reactive than carbon, which is why carbon can extract it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The series is remembered as a list without a direction, so the carbon comparison is read the wrong way round; the metal being produced also feels like it ought to be the stronger one.
misconceptions.correction: Carbon can only take oxygen from a metal below it in the series. A successful carbon reduction shows the metal is less reactive than carbon, not more.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium ribbon is burned in air and a white powder is left behind. Which statement about the magnesium is correct?

options.text: The magnesium gains oxygen, so the magnesium is oxidised.
options.rationale: Metals react with oxygen to produce metal oxides, and the reaction is an oxidation because the metal gains oxygen.

options.text: The magnesium gains oxygen, so it has been reduced.
options.rationale: The student has the observation right but attaches the wrong label, having learnt the pair of terms without their direction.

options.text: The magnesium and the oxygen are simply mixed.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who sees the same lump of metal still present and treats the powder as a mixture rather than a new compound.

options.text: The magnesium is used up, so it must be reduced.
options.rationale: Reads 'reduced' with its everyday meaning of made smaller, and points at the metal being used up. The label depends on oxygen, not on how much solid is left, and burning magnesium in fact gains mass as it takes in oxygen.

mcqs.stem: Copper is heated in air and a black solid forms on the surface. What is the black solid and what has happened to the copper?

options.text: Copper oxide, though this is not an oxidation.
options.rationale: Selected by a student who requires a flame before the word oxidation can be used, since copper does not visibly burn.

options.text: Copper oxide; the copper has been oxidised.
options.rationale: Copper reacts with oxygen to give copper oxide, and gaining oxygen is oxidation, however gently the reaction proceeds.

options.text: A mixture of copper and air joined on.
options.rationale: Treats the black layer as trapped air rather than as a compound with a fixed composition.

options.text: Copper oxide; the copper has been reduced.
options.rationale: Identifies the product correctly but reverses the two redox labels.

mcqs.stem: In the reaction 2CuO + C -> 2Cu + CO2, which substance is reduced, and why?

options.text: Carbon, because it gains oxygen in this.
options.rationale: Applies the definition backwards, treating gain of oxygen as reduction.

options.text: Copper oxide, because the mass falls.
options.rationale: Uses the everyday sense of reduce and points at the mass change rather than at the oxygen.

options.text: Copper oxide, because it loses oxygen.
options.rationale: Reduction in terms of oxygen is loss of oxygen; the copper oxide gives up its oxygen to the carbon.

options.text: Carbon, since it removes the oxygen atoms.
options.rationale: Hears 'the carbon reduces the oxide' and reads the verb as describing what happens to the carbon.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen is correct?

options.text: Reduction is gain of oxygen; oxidation is loss of it.
options.rationale: The two terms are remembered as a pair of opposites but assigned the wrong way round.

options.text: Reduction means the mass of the solid gets smaller.
options.rationale: Substitutes the everyday meaning of reduce for the chemical definition.

options.text: A reaction shows oxidation or reduction, never both.
options.rationale: Files the two terms as alternatives rather than as two halves of a single transfer of oxygen.

options.text: Oxidation is gain of oxygen; reduction is loss.
options.rationale: This is the definition required by the specification: reduction and oxidation explained in terms of loss or gain of oxygen.

mcqs.stem: A metal reacts with another substance. What happens to the metal atoms during the reaction?

options.text: The metal atoms lose electrons and form positive ions.
options.rationale: When metals react with other substances the metal atoms form positive ions by losing their outer electrons.

options.text: The metal atoms gain electrons to form negative ions.
options.rationale: Assumes the reactive metal takes electrons rather than gives them, which feels like the more aggressive option.

options.text: The metal atoms gain protons and become positive.
options.rationale: Links positive charge to protons correctly but moves the wrong particle.

options.text: The metal atoms stay neutral and just join on.
options.rationale: Pictures reaction as particles sticking together with nothing changing inside the atom.

mcqs.stem: The reactivity of a metal is related to which property of its atoms?

options.text: Its tendency to grip its own electrons.
options.rationale: Reads reactive as strong, and holding on tightly sounds like the stronger behaviour.

options.text: Its tendency to form positive ions.
options.rationale: The specification states that the reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions.

options.text: How dense and hard the metal is.
options.rationale: Borrows visible physical properties to explain a chemical property with no visible cause.

options.text: The ability to form negative ions.
options.rationale: Right idea of ion formation, wrong sign of charge for a metal.

mcqs.stem: From their reactions with water and with dilute acids, which metal is placed highest in the reactivity series?

options.text: Copper, as it will not react with dilute acid.
options.rationale: Reads the series upside down, so the metal that does nothing is placed at the top.

options.text: Calcium, since it loses two electrons per atom.
options.rationale: Assumes that losing more electrons must mean greater reactivity.

options.text: Potassium, as it reacts fast with cold water.
options.rationale: Potassium reacts most vigorously of all these metals with cold water, so it stands at the top of the order.

options.text: Zinc, since its atoms have most mass.
options.rationale: Ranks the metals by relative atomic mass instead of by their reactions.

mcqs.stem: The non-metals hydrogen and carbon are often included in the reactivity series. Why?

options.text: They are included because they are unusual metals.
options.rationale: Assumes anything listed alongside metals must itself be a metal.

options.text: They are placed there because every ore holds carbon.
options.rationale: Confuses the coke used in a furnace with the composition of the ore itself.

options.text: They show that carbon extracts any metal from its ore.
options.rationale: Over-generalises the one extraction method studied to every metal in the list.

options.text: They are reference points to compare metals with.
options.rationale: Including them lets a metal be judged as above or below carbon or hydrogen, which is what predicts extraction and acid reactions.

mcqs.stem: A strip of magnesium is left in copper(II) sulfate solution. A pink-brown solid forms on the strip and the blue colour fades. Why?

options.text: Magnesium is more reactive, so it displaces the copper.
options.rationale: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound, so magnesium takes the place of copper and copper metal is deposited.

options.text: Copper is more reactive, so it displaces magnesium.
options.rationale: Uses the reactivity series upside down and lets the less reactive metal do the displacing.

options.text: Both are metals, so they simply swap places.
options.rationale: Treats displacement as automatic between any two metals, with no condition attached.

options.text: The blue fades because the solution was diluted.
options.rationale: Explains the colour change as a physical dilution rather than as a chemical change.

mcqs.stem: Which mixture will produce a displacement reaction?

options.text: Copper added to zinc sulfate solution.
options.rationale: The reverse pairing, chosen by a student reading the series in the wrong direction.

options.text: Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution.
options.rationale: Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series, so zinc displaces copper from the solution.

options.text: Iron added to magnesium sulfate solution.
options.rationale: Assumes any metal will displace any other, ignoring the order of reactivity.

options.text: Copper added to iron(III) sulfate solution.
options.rationale: Puts copper above iron because copper atoms are heavier.

mcqs.stem: Which metal reacts with cold water at room temperature to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen?

options.text: Zinc, which bubbles steadily in cold water.
options.rationale: Generalises from the alkali metal demonstrations to every metal in the list.

options.text: Copper, used in pipes that carry water.
options.rationale: Reads constant contact with water as evidence that copper reacts with it.

options.text: Sodium, which fizzes on the water surface.
options.rationale: Sodium is above magnesium in the reactivity series and reacts readily with cold water to give sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.

options.text: Iron, because it rusts whenever it gets wet.
options.rationale: Treats rusting as the same reaction as the cold water test being compared here.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. What are the products?

options.text: Magnesium oxide and hydrogen gas.
options.rationale: Expects an oxide because metal oxides dominate the earlier work on oxidation.

options.text: Magnesium chloride and water only.
options.rationale: Applies the acid plus base neutralisation pattern to a metal.

options.text: Magnesium chloride and chlorine gas.
options.rationale: Takes the gas from the name of the acid rather than from the reaction.

options.text: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
options.rationale: A metal reacting with a dilute acid gives a salt and hydrogen; with hydrochloric acid the salt is the chloride.

mcqs.stem: A piece of copper is left in dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. Which statement describes what happens?

options.text: Nothing happens, because copper is below hydrogen.
options.rationale: Copper is the least reactive metal in the list and lies below hydrogen, so it does not displace hydrogen from a dilute acid.

options.text: It fizzes steadily and gives off hydrogen.
options.rationale: Applies the metal plus acid rule to every metal without exception.

options.text: It reacts, but too slowly for bubbles to show.
options.rationale: Cannot accept no reaction as an answer and assumes an unseen slow change.

options.text: It dissolves slowly and turns the acid blue.
options.rationale: Recalls that copper compounds are blue and assumes the acid must be dissolving the metal.

mcqs.stem: Potassium reacts far more vigorously with cold water than magnesium does. What best explains this difference?

options.text: Potassium holds on to its electrons more strongly.
options.rationale: Reverses the reasoning by treating a strong grip on electrons as the cause of reactivity.

options.text: Potassium loses its outer electron more readily.
options.rationale: Reactivity is related to the tendency to form positive ions, and potassium gives up its outer electron much more easily than magnesium.

options.text: Potassium loses two electrons, magnesium one.
options.rationale: Counts electrons and gets the counts the wrong way round, assuming more lost means more reactive.

options.text: Potassium is a softer, less dense metal.
options.rationale: Offers a physical property in place of a reason based on ion formation.

mcqs.stem: Metals X and Y are added to dilute acid. X fizzes vigorously while Y fizzes only slowly. What does this show about the atoms?

options.text: Y gives up its outer electrons more easily than X.
options.rationale: Matches the slower reaction to the easier electron loss, reversing the relationship.

options.text: X can form negative ions more readily than Y.
options.rationale: Correct comparison but the wrong charge for a metal ion.

options.text: X forms positive ions more readily than Y.
options.rationale: The vigour of the reaction with dilute acid reflects how readily the metal atoms give up electrons to form positive ions.

options.text: X has more electrons in total than Y has.
options.rationale: Uses the total electron count rather than the ease of losing the outer ones.

mcqs.stem: Four metals are added to dilute acid. P bubbles very fast, S bubbles moderately, Q bubbles slowly and R shows no change. What is the order of reactivity, most reactive first?

options.text: R, Q, S, P - slowest bubbling means most reactive.
options.rationale: Reads the evidence in reverse, ranking the calmest metal highest.

options.text: R, P, S, Q - no reaction at all means most reactive.
options.rationale: Hears unreactive as strong and promotes the metal that resisted the acid.

options.text: P, S, Q only - R cannot be placed in the series.
options.rationale: Discards the negative result instead of treating it as evidence.

options.text: P, S, Q, R - fastest bubbling is most reactive.
options.rationale: Rate of reaction with the same dilute acid ranks the metals directly, and a metal showing no change is the least reactive of the set.

mcqs.stem: In separate tests, metal A displaces metal B from its sulfate solution, and metal B displaces metal C from its sulfate solution. What can be concluded?

options.text: A is the most reactive of the three and C the least.
options.rationale: The two results chain together into one order, A above B above C, which is exactly how an order of reactivity is deduced from results.

options.text: C is the most reactive and A the least reactive.
options.rationale: Reads displacement in the wrong direction, so the displaced metal is ranked highest.

options.text: A and B are ordered, but C cannot be placed.
options.rationale: Refuses to combine the two results, so the third metal is left unplaced.

options.text: All three are equally reactive as all reacted.
options.rationale: Treats any reaction occurring as evidence that the metals are alike.

mcqs.stem: Gold is found in the Earth as the metal itself rather than as a compound. Why?

options.text: Gold was reduced by carbon deep underground long ago.
options.rationale: Applies the extraction story to explain a metal that was never combined in the first place.

options.text: Gold is unreactive, so it does not form compounds.
options.rationale: Unreactive metals such as gold are found as the metal itself; most other metals are found as compounds needing chemical extraction.

options.text: Gold is very rare, so too little of it can react.
options.rationale: Uses scarcity, learnt alongside gold, as though it were a chemical reason.

options.text: Gold is so dense that it sinks below the ores.
options.rationale: Borrows the density argument from gold panning to explain its chemical state.

mcqs.stem: Iron oxide is heated with carbon and iron metal is obtained. Why does this method work for iron?

options.text: Iron is more reactive than the carbon.
options.rationale: Gets the comparison the wrong way round while still naming the right factor.

options.text: Carbon reduces every metal oxide.
options.rationale: Treats carbon reduction as universal, so no comparison is needed.

options.text: Iron is less reactive than carbon.
options.rationale: Metals less reactive than carbon can be extracted from their oxides by reduction with carbon.

options.text: The carbon melts the iron out of the ore.
options.rationale: Sees a hot furnace pouring molten metal and reads the change as melting.

mcqs.stem: Which metal cannot be extracted from its oxide by reduction with carbon?

options.text: Copper, which is well below carbon.
options.rationale: Inverts the rule, ruling out the metal that carbon can in fact reduce.

options.text: Zinc, since carbon cannot reduce it.
options.rationale: Names a metal below carbon, missing the comparison that decides the method.

options.text: Iron, whose ore must be melted first.
options.rationale: Substitutes melting for the chemical reduction that actually frees the metal.

options.text: Potassium, which is above carbon.
options.rationale: Potassium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen from potassium oxide.

mcqs.stem: What does the term reduction mean when a metal is obtained from its oxide?

options.text: The oxide loses its oxygen and metal is left behind.
options.rationale: Reduction involves the loss of oxygen, which is exactly what happens to the oxide during extraction.

options.text: The oxide gains extra oxygen from the carbon.
options.rationale: Applies the definition backwards, so oxygen is added rather than removed.

options.text: The mass of the solid in the furnace falls.
options.rationale: Names a consequence and mistakes it for the definition.

options.text: The oxide melts and the metal simply runs out.
options.rationale: Describes a physical separation instead of a chemical reaction.

mcqs.stem: A furnace is charged with lead(II) oxide and carbon. The reaction is 2PbO + C -> 2Pb + CO2. Which statement about this process is correct?

options.text: Lead lies above carbon in the reactivity series.
options.rationale: Reverses the comparison, which would make this extraction impossible.

options.text: Lead is below carbon in the reactivity series.
options.rationale: Carbon has taken the oxygen from the lead oxide, which can only happen if lead is less reactive than carbon.

options.text: Carbon is reduced and lead oxide is oxidised.
options.rationale: Swaps the two labels, prompted by carbon being called the reducing agent.

options.text: Only reduction occurs; nothing is oxidised.
options.rationale: Overlooks that the oxygen removed must be gained by something else.

mcqs.stem: A student is told that a metal M is found in the Earth as its oxide and that M is obtained by heating that oxide with carbon. What can be deduced about M?

options.text: M must be more reactive than carbon.
options.rationale: Gets the direction of the comparison wrong.

options.text: M is just as unreactive as gold.
options.rationale: Confuses being extractable with being found native; M was found combined.

options.text: M is less reactive than carbon is.
options.rationale: Only a metal below carbon can have its oxygen taken by carbon, so the stated method places M below carbon.

options.text: M's reactivity does not matter at all.
options.rationale: Assumes carbon reduction works for every metal, so nothing can be deduced.

mcqs.stem: In the reaction 2Fe2O3 + 3C -> 4Fe + 3CO2, which substance is oxidised?

options.text: Carbon, because it loses oxygen here.
options.rationale: Names the right substance for the wrong reason, having reversed the oxygen change.

options.text: Iron oxide, because it gains oxygen.
options.rationale: Applies the definition of oxidation to the substance that in fact loses oxygen.

options.text: Iron oxide, because it loses its oxygen.
options.rationale: Describes the oxygen change correctly but labels it oxidation instead of reduction.

options.text: Carbon, because it gains oxygen.
options.rationale: The carbon gains oxygen to form carbon dioxide, and gain of oxygen is oxidation.

mcqs.stem: In terms of electrons, which statement is correct?

options.text: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons.

options.text: Oxidation is the gain of electrons and reduction the loss.
options.rationale: Carries 'gain' across from the oxygen definition of oxidation.

options.text: Oxidation is the loss of protons and reduction the gain.
options.rationale: Swaps the particle, because protons are the ones linked to charge.

options.text: Oxidation and reduction both involve losing electrons.
options.rationale: Recalls only half of the definition and applies it to both species.

mcqs.stem: In the reaction Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, which species is oxidised and why?

options.text: Zinc, since it gains two electrons.
options.rationale: Identifies the right species but reverses the direction of electron transfer.

options.text: Zinc, because it loses its two electrons.
options.rationale: Zn becomes Zn2+, a loss of two electrons, and oxidation is the loss of electrons.

options.text: The copper ion, because it loses electrons.
options.rationale: Assigns electron loss to both species, so the ion is labelled oxidised too.

options.text: The copper ion, as it becomes a metal.
options.rationale: Picks the visible change and labels it oxidation.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Which is the correct ionic equation?

options.text: Mg + CuSO4 -> MgSO4 + Cu
options.rationale: Copies the full symbol equation, leaving the unchanged sulfate ions in place.

options.text: 2Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu
options.rationale: Tries to fix the charges with a big number, which balances neither charge nor the magnesium atoms.

options.text: Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg2+ + Cu
options.rationale: Only the species that change are shown; magnesium loses two electrons and the copper ion gains them.

options.text: Mg + Cu2+ -> Mg+ + Cu
options.rationale: Shows the right species but gives magnesium the wrong charge, so charge does not balance.

mcqs.stem: Which half equation shows a species being reduced?

options.text: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-, a gain of two electrons.
options.rationale: Sees electrons in the equation and calls it a gain regardless of which side they are on.

options.text: Mg + 2e- -> Mg2+, electrons are taken in.
options.rationale: Sees electrons on the left and stops there, without checking that the charges do not balance and that magnesium is becoming an ion, not an atom.

options.text: Cu2+ -> Cu + 2e-, showing a gain of two.
options.rationale: Writes the electrons on the wrong side, so neither charge nor the direction of transfer is right.

options.text: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, a gain of electrons.
options.rationale: Electrons appear on the left and are taken in by the ion, and gain of electrons is reduction.
